newsitem.title: USA: TWA crash "consistent" with fuel explosion - NTSB.
newsitem.headline: TWA crash "consistent" with fuel explosion - NTSB.

text.p: The National Transportation Safety Board said on Friday evidence from the crash of TWA Flight 800 was "consistent" with a fuel tank explosion, and it proposed new steps to prevent volatile fuel and air mixtures.
"The reconstruction thus far shows outward deformation ... of the internal components of the tank that are consistent with an explosion originating within the tank," the NTSB said.

In a written statement to the Federal Aviation Administration, the NTSB recommended modifications to aircraft design to prevent such fuel tank explosions. The FAA said it would urgently review the board's request.
The Paris-bound TWA flight exploded shortly after takeoff from New York's Kennedy Airport July 17 and plunged into the Atlantic Ocean, killing all 230 people on board.

The NTSB said parts of the Boeing 747 recovered and identified so far showed no evidence of bomb or missile damage. More than 90 percent of the wreckage has been salvaged from the waters off Long Island, New York.

However, the NTSB stopped short of flatly declaring the crash a mechanical accident, saying: "The investigation into what might have provided the source of ignition of the fuel-air mixture (including a bomb or missile) in the centre wing tank is continuing."

The NTSB recommended the FAA consider aircraft design modifications, such as fire-extinguishing systems. It also recommended the addition of insulation between heat-generating equipment, such as air-conditioning ducts, and the fuel tanks.

The board also urged the FAA to consider a rule requiring an appropriate amount of fuel be kept in the centre wing tank of the B-747. Whenever possible the fuel should be cool. There should be proper monitoring and maintenance of the tank's temperature, it said.

"The Board believes that the FAA should require modification of the CWT (center wing tank) of B-747 airplanes and the fuel tanks of other airplanes that are located near heat sources to incorporate temperature probes and cockpit fuel tank temperature displays to permit determination of fuel tank temperatures," the statement said.
The NTSB on Saturday will brief families of the victims of Flight 800 to update them on the progress of the investigation.
